fields.title: From Users to Requests
fields.keyTakeaway: A product plan is translated into load by four multiplications, and the main thing in it is not the average, but the peak.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Marketing promises 200 thousand new users per month. Is this a lot for the system or not?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Without translating into system units, this question has no answer, and the PM either over-insures or brings a surprise to the team. A campaign that engineers found out about three days in advance is a typical cause of failure at the moment of maximum attention to the product.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: [[load|Load]] is measured in [[rps|requests per second]]. Translating from product metrics is done in four steps, and the PM has all the data for it.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Step 1. Daily active users.** Not total registered — active.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Step 2. Actions per user per session.** Opening the app is not one request, but ten to twenty: feed, catalog, cart, profile.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Step 3. Average per second.** Multiplied, divided by 86,400.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **Step 4. [[peak-to-average-ratio|Peak]].** The average means nothing: the system must withstand the peak. For consumer products the coefficient is usually 3–6, for B2B with a working day — up to 10.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: Example on Polka: 180 thousand active daily, about 25 requests per session, 1.4 sessions — this is roughly 6.3 million requests per day, 73 per second on average. With a peak coefficient of 5 — about 370 at the peak.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: The second concept is **[[concurrency|concurrency]]**: how many operations are executed simultaneously. It is more important than RPS where operations are slow. One hundred requests per second at 50 ms each is 5 concurrent. One hundred requests at 2 seconds each — 200 concurrent, and this is already a question of the number of database connections.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: Translation rule: concurrency ≈ RPS × operation duration.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: TV campaign: a spike is expected at the moment the ad airs. Calculated as follows.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: Prime time ad, audience about 2 million, expected conversion 0.5% — 10 thousand people. They do not arrive evenly: 60% in the first 10 minutes. That is 600 people per minute, 10 new sessions per second, each with 25 requests in the first half-minute — about 500 additional requests per second on top of the usual 370.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Doubling of the peak. With this figure we went to the team, and the conversation took twenty minutes instead of a week of clarifications.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: Reverse case: a partner newsletter to 900 stores "report is ready" caused a morning spike in the dashboard — the exact Monday peak from block `DS1`. No one calculated it in advance back then, even though the newsletter was planned.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: A back-of-the-envelope estimate gives an order of magnitude, and this is enough for the decision "to prepare or not". Only load testing shows the exact behavior under load.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: A product plan is translated into load by four multiplications, and the main thing in it is not the average, but the peak.
